title: Zoo Lions Act More Like Wild Lions With a Feast-and-Fast Menu
summary:
Wild lions do not eat at the same time every day. Sometimes they have a big meal after a successful hunt, and then they go days without food. Scientists in Australia wanted to know what happens when zoo lions eat on a schedule that is more like that.

Researchers from Adelaide University worked with Monarto Safari Park in South Australia. They studied three adult male African lions. The lions were already on a feeding plan with times of eating and times of not eating. Then animal care staff added something new: every nine days, the lions got a whole animal to eat instead of just pieces of meat.

Eight infrared cameras recorded the lions day and night for three months. On whole-animal days, the lions spent almost three times as long eating as usual. They pulled, tore and worked at their food for long stretches, just as wild lions do.

After the big meal, the lions rested much longer. Then, as the days went by, they slowly became more active again. Scientists said this pattern of feasting, resting and then moving more closely matched what is seen in wild lions.

"Wild lions don't eat at the same time every day," said lead researcher Lesia Hryhorenko. She said whole meals give lions a chance to use natural behaviors that are an important part of their lives.

The team also watched pacing, when an animal walks back and forth. Pacing did not go up just because the lions were hungry. It rose most around predictable events, like when keepers arrived.

The study was published in the journal Applied Animal Behaviour Science.
why_it_matters: Understanding how feeding routines affect animals can help zoos give lions lives that feel more natural and healthy.

background_read: In the wild, lions hunt, and because hunts do not always succeed, they may eat a lot at once and then go days without food.
Zoos and safari parks try to give animals chances to act naturally, which keepers call enrichment.
Scientists often use cameras to watch animals without disturbing them and to record what they do day and night.
Pacing, or walking back and forth, is a behavior keepers watch closely because it can show how an animal is feeling about its routine.
